body.text: Dancing is illegal in Iran, but an underground ballet network is defying the regime
With curtains drawn, furniture pushed against the wall, and chairs used as makeshift ballet barres, a group of young dancers in Iran prepare to begin their pointe class in secret.
For many of them, it is a quiet but fierce act of defiance against a regime that has long outlawed dancing for women.
Running these prohibited classes is US-Iranian ballerina Tara Ghassemieh, also known as the Persian Swan.
"You have to be so incredibly brave and have such a love for the art form even to put on shoes and learn it in your own living room or basement," she said.
The 1979 Iranian revolution outlawed dancing for women in public — seeing it as sinful, seductive, and tied to Western influence.
The regime destroyed archives, shut down dance academies, and even had the Iranian National Ballet Company dissolved, with dancers fleeing to neighbouring countries for safety.
Ms Ghassemieh has heard their grim stories.
"They were met with machine guns in their rehearsal space and told 'you are done dancing,' and they meant it," she said.
The oppression struck a nerve with Ms Ghassemieh, who, for the last three years, has been teaching ballet to Iranian dancers from her home in California.
But she was not oblivious to the risks.
"If you're caught dancing, especially in public, you can be thrown in jail and you can be handed a death sentence,"
"So it is a matter of life and death. Or it can be a fine, which you then pay off with the bribe. It's extremely corrupt."
Her work is part of a broader underground network called Dancers of Iran, an organisation that supports, educates and connects Iranian dancers inside the country and around the world.
It was founded by Tina Bararian, an Iranian Canadian dancer and choreographer based in Toronto, whose family fled Iran to Australia when she was young and eventually settled in Canada.
Seeing few other Iranian dancers in her classes growing up, she was desperate to learn more about the dancing culture of her homeland.
"When I travelled back to Iran, I really wanted to connect with the dancers who are dancing underground," Ms Bararian said.

"But at that time, there wasn't a lot of trust amongst the people because obviously if they talked publicly that they're dancers or that they're practising dance, they could have gotten into trouble."
Students' safety threatened
Dancers of Iran has spread across the country since it was founded in 2021.
But students know that logging onto a virtual class is a safety risk.
Ms Bararian personally monitors the classes for any signs of suspicious participants.

"If an account approaches us who has zero followers, sadly, I would never reply back to them … just because I'm not sure whether that's a real person or that's someone from the [Iranian] government trying to sneak in," she said.
Anyone associated with the art inside Iran knows to tread carefully.
One dance teacher in Tehran who spoke to the ABC on condition of anonymity said she does not advertise her classes for fear of consequences.
She teaches over 200 students in a secret studio — and laments the fact that their talents cannot be displayed to the world.

"There are so many talented students here, so many beautiful dancers … but they reach this opportunity to have classes so late in their lives that it's almost too late for them to get something out of it," she said.
Dancers imprisoned for viral videos
Punishments for perceived acts of defiance through dance are severe in Iran.
In 2023, a young Iranian couple were sentenced to ten years in prison for posting a video of themselves dancing in Tehran.
About a month later, five young women were detained and forced to write public apologies for posting a viral TikTok dance in which they weren't wearing hijabs.

They had been dancing as part of the Women, Life, Freedom movement — a grassroots resistance campaign following the 2022 death in custody of Jina Mahsa Amini, who had been arrested for wearing her hijab incorrectly.
Ms Bararian said these stories of detention were far from isolated.
She has spoken to one dancer who still lives inside Iran, who has been arrested multiple times for running classes.

"He once told me that if he was a drug dealer, it would have been easier than being a dancer inside Iran. Because at least if he was a drug dealer, his sentences would have been less harsh," she said.
Supporting dancers inside Iran

As someone fortunate enough to grow up dancing freely, Ms Ghassemieh feels a responsibility to give back to her community, especially to those who have not known what it is like to perform on stage, or even in public.
"I should not be the first in 2026. The only reason I am is due to suppression and lack of access to the art form for even the Iranians that were able to leave Iran," she said.
She says the stories of her dancers inspire her to keep teaching.
One student in particular had a gut-wrenching tale to tell.
"When the 12-day war happened with Israel [in June 2025], all she grabbed were her pointe shoes and her phone and said, 'I'm good to go'," Ms Ghassemieh said.
"When she had to flee her apartment building, that's literally all she needed."
The Persian Swan is desperate to bring the plight of these hidden dancers to the world stage.
She has even choreographed a piece called The White Feather, documenting the dissolution of the Iranian National Ballet.
Performed in a hijab that is ripped off halfway through, it is a symbol of solidarity with the Women, Life, Freedom resistance movement.
The next generation of Iranian performers
Ms Bararian hopes ballet will one day be freely performed across her homeland, and believes her network can send a message of strength and solidarity to the next generation of Iranian ballerinas.
"You might have to work harder than a person who is privileged enough to take dance classes in a free country, but that doesn't mean that you can't dream," she said.
Ms Ghassemieh believes one day she will stamp her own pointe shoe on a stage in Iran — a symbol of defiance and fierce resolve that she hopes to pass on to her students.
"If you have that ache in your heart and you have that fire and that pull to dance … then never let anybody tell you cannot be a dancer," she said.
"Never stop dancing in whatever capacity you safely can learn this art form. If it's calling you, then it's meant for you."
